examples.name: Blink
examples.description: Blink the on-board LED once per second.

lesson.learn: How every Arduino sketch is built: setup() runs once, loop() repeats forever. You'll switch a pin on and off.
lesson.wiring: Nothing to wire: most ESP32 dev boards have a blue LED on GPIO 2 (LED_BUILTIN). Optional: an LED with a 220 Ω resistor from GPIO 2 to GND.
lesson.how: pinMode() makes the pin an output. In loop(), digitalWrite(HIGH) turns the LED on, delay(1000) waits one second, LOW turns it off.
tryThis: Make it blink twice as fast.
Make it stay on for 100 ms and off for 900 ms: a heartbeat.
Blink an SOS: three short, three long, three short.

examples.name: BlinkWithoutDelay
examples.description: Blink the LED with millis() so the loop never blocks.

lesson.learn: How to time things without delay(), so your sketch can do several jobs at once.
lesson.wiring: Nothing to wire: uses the built-in LED.
lesson.how: millis() counts milliseconds since start. Each loop checks whether INTERVAL_MS has passed since the last change; only then it flips the LED. Nothing ever waits.
tryThis: Change INTERVAL_MS to 100.
Print a message to Serial every 2 seconds while the LED keeps blinking.
Blink a second LED at a different speed.

examples.name: Button
examples.description: Read a button with the internal pull-up resistor.

lesson.learn: How to read an input: a button, with the chip's built-in pull-up resistor.
lesson.wiring: Nothing to wire: GPIO 0 is the BOOT button on ESP32 dev boards (FLASH on NodeMCU). Or wire your own button from a GPIO to GND and change BUTTON_PIN.
lesson.how: INPUT_PULLUP holds the pin HIGH; pressing the button connects it to GND, so digitalRead() returns LOW while pressed.
tryThis: Turn the LED on while the button is pressed.
Count presses and print the count (hint: react only when it changes from HIGH to LOW).
Make each press toggle the LED.

examples.name: AnalogRead
examples.description: Read a voltage on an analog pin and print it.

lesson.learn: How to measure a voltage, the way you read sensors like potentiometers, light sensors and soil-moisture probes.
lesson.wiring: ESP32: potentiometer middle pin to GPIO 34, outer pins to 3.3 V and GND. ESP8266: middle pin to A0. Never put more than 3.3 V on a pin.
lesson.how: analogRead() turns the voltage into a number: 0–4095 on the ESP32, 0–1023 on the ESP8266. The sketch prints it to the Serial Monitor.
tryThis: Open the Serial plotter and turn the knob.
Use map() to print a percentage from 0 to 100.
Turn on the LED when the value is above half.

examples.name: Fade
examples.description: Fade the LED in and out with PWM (analogWrite).

lesson.learn: How PWM makes an LED look dimmer by switching it very fast.
lesson.wiring: Nothing to wire: fades the built-in LED.
lesson.how: analogWrite(pin, duty) sets brightness from 0 (off) to 255 (full). The loop raises and lowers duty a little at a time.
tryThis: Make the fade slower.
Fade only up, then jump back to off.
Control the brightness with a potentiometer (combine with AnalogRead).

examples.name: SerialEcho
examples.description: Echo everything received on the serial port.

lesson.learn: How the board can receive text from your phone, not only send it.
lesson.wiring: Nothing to wire. Open the Serial Monitor at 115200 baud and send something.
lesson.how: Serial.available() says how many characters arrived; Serial.read() takes them one at a time and the sketch sends each one back.
tryThis: Reply in capitals (hint: toupper()).
Turn the LED on when you send 1 and off when you send 0.
Read whole lines with Serial.readStringUntil('\n').

examples.name: HelloSerial
examples.description: Print a counter to the Serial Monitor every second.

lesson.learn: How to print messages and numbers from the board, the most useful debugging tool you have.
lesson.wiring: Nothing to wire. Open the Serial Monitor at 115200 baud.
lesson.how: Serial.begin(115200) starts the connection; Serial.print() and Serial.println() send text and numbers.
tryThis: Print the time since start with millis().
Print a count-down from 10.
Print two numbers on one line separated by a space and open the plotter.

examples.name: WiFiScan
examples.description: List the Wi-Fi networks in range.

lesson.learn: How the board sees the Wi-Fi networks around it.
lesson.wiring: Nothing to wire. Open the Serial Monitor.
lesson.how: WiFi.scanNetworks() searches and returns how many networks it found; WiFi.SSID(i) and WiFi.RSSI(i) give each name and signal strength in dBm (closer to 0 is stronger).
tryThis: Print only networks stronger than -70 dBm.
Count how many networks are open (no password).
Blink the LED once per network found.

examples.name: WiFiConnect
examples.description: Join a Wi-Fi network and print the IP address.

lesson.learn: How to join your Wi-Fi network, the first step for any internet project.
lesson.wiring: Nothing to wire. Put your network name and password in the sketch. Most boards only use 2.4 GHz networks.
lesson.how: WiFi.begin() starts connecting; the loop waits until WiFi.status() is WL_CONNECTED, then prints the IP address the router gave the board.
tryThis: Blink the LED fast while connecting and keep it on once connected.
Print the signal strength with WiFi.RSSI().
Reconnect automatically if the connection drops.

examples.name: HttpGet
examples.description: Fetch a web page over HTTP.

lesson.learn: How to fetch a web page or an API from the internet.
lesson.wiring: Nothing to wire. Set your Wi-Fi name and password first.
lesson.how: After connecting, HTTPClient sends a GET request; the response code (200 means OK) and the page text are printed.
tryThis: Fetch a different URL.
Print only the first 200 characters of the reply.
Fetch the page again every 30 seconds.

examples.name: WebServerHello
examples.description: A tiny web server that answers Hello.

lesson.learn: How the board can host its own web page that anyone on your Wi-Fi can open.
lesson.wiring: Nothing to wire. Set your Wi-Fi details, upload, then open the IP address shown in the Serial Monitor in your phone's browser.
lesson.how: The web server waits for browsers to connect; server.on("/") says what to send back. server.handleClient() in loop() answers each request.
tryThis: Change the page text and add a heading with <h1>.
Show millis() on the page so it changes when you refresh.
Add a second page at /led that turns the LED on.

examples.name: NtpClock
examples.description: Sync the clock over NTP and print the time.

lesson.learn: How the board gets the real date and time from the internet.
lesson.wiring: Nothing to wire. Set your Wi-Fi details and your time zone.
lesson.how: configTime() asks internet time servers (NTP) for the time; after that the board keeps time itself and the sketch prints it every second.
tryThis: Print only the hour and minute.
Turn the LED on at a set time.
Print the day of the week.

examples.name: WiFiAccessPointLed
examples.description: Start a Wi-Fi hotspot with a web page that switches the LED.

lesson.learn: How the board can make its own Wi-Fi hotspot, with a web page that controls a pin.
lesson.wiring: Nothing to wire: switches the built-in LED. Join the Wi-Fi "EspSketch-LED" (password circuithub) on your phone, then open 192.168.4.1.
lesson.how: WiFi.softAP() starts a hotspot; the web server sends a page with On and Off buttons, and each button's address switches the LED.
tryThis: Change the hotspot name and password.
Add a Blink button.
Show the LED's current state on the page.

examples.name: BLEScan
examples.description: List Bluetooth Low Energy devices nearby.

lesson.learn: How the ESP32 finds Bluetooth Low Energy devices nearby: phones, watches, fitness bands, beacons.
lesson.wiring: Nothing to wire. Open the Serial Monitor.
lesson.how: BLEDevice::init() starts Bluetooth; the scanner listens for SCAN_SECONDS and lists each device's address, name and signal strength.
tryThis: Print only devices that have a name.
Turn the LED on when a device is very close (RSSI above -50).
Scan for 10 seconds instead of 5.

examples.name: DeepSleepTimer
examples.description: Sleep for ten seconds, wake up, repeat.

lesson.learn: How to save battery: the board sleeps, using almost no power, and wakes up on a timer.
lesson.wiring: ESP32: nothing to wire. ESP8266: connect GPIO16 (D0) to RST with a wire so the timer can wake the board.
lesson.how: The board goes to deep sleep for SLEEP_SECONDS. Waking up is a restart, so the sketch runs from setup() again; loop() never runs.
tryThis: Sleep for 30 seconds instead.
Blink the LED once each time it wakes.
Count wake-ups (ESP32: use a variable marked RTC_DATA_ATTR).

examples.name: TouchSensor
examples.description: Read a capacitive touch pin (classic ESP32 only).

lesson.learn: How the ESP32 can feel a finger without a button, using a touch pin.
lesson.wiring: Attach a wire or a piece of foil to GPIO 4 (touch pin T0) and touch it.
lesson.how: touchRead() returns a number that drops when you touch the pin; below THRESHOLD counts as touched.
tryThis: Watch the values in the Serial plotter and pick a better THRESHOLD.
Make a touch toggle the LED.
Use two touch pins as + and - buttons.

examples.name: SavedCounter
examples.description: Count restarts and keep the count in flash.

lesson.learn: How to remember a value after the power goes off by saving it in flash memory.
lesson.wiring: Nothing to wire. Press the board's EN/RST button to restart it and watch the count.
lesson.how: On each start the sketch reads the count from flash, adds one, saves it back and prints it. ESP32 uses Preferences; ESP8266 uses EEPROM.
tryThis: Reset the count when the BOOT button is held during start-up.
Also save the time since the last start.
Save your Wi-Fi name in flash instead of in the code.
